questions.question: What is extended reality (XR)?
questions.reference_answer: XR stands for extended reality. It is an umbrella term, not one specific technology: it covers all immersive technologies, present or future, such as AR, VR and MR. The X can be read as part of 'extended' or as a variable that takes the values A (augmented), V (virtual) or M (mixed).
must_have: XR = extended reality
an umbrella term, not a specific technology
covers the immersive technologies AR, VR, MR

questions.question: what does immersion mean in VR?
questions.reference_answer: Immersion is the objective degree to which a VR system and application projects stimuli onto the user's sensory receptors in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive and plot informing (the definition of Slater and Wilbur). It is the technological, system side of the experience: what the technology provides. Earlier, in lecture 1, 'immersive' is introduced as an experience through the sense organs that appears real, so that the user cannot tell the environment from the real one.
must_have: an objective degree: what the system projects onto the user's senses
the technological (system) side, not the user's state of mind
described by qualities such as extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, plot informing (naming some is enough)

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

sources.quote: This is a definition which was originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur.

questions.question: What is presence?
questions.reference_answer: Presence is a psychological state or subjective perception in which, although part or all of what a person experiences is generated or filtered by technology, the person's perception fails to acknowledge the role of the technology (definition of the International Society for Presence Research). In VR it means the user perceives the computer-generated stimuli as if they came from the real world: the feeling of really being in the virtual world. Creating a high degree of presence is the overall goal of a VR system.
must_have: a psychological state / subjective perception of the user
the user does not notice the role of the technology: the virtual world is felt as real ('being there')

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: What it says is, presence is a psychological state or subjective perception in which even though part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by and/or filtered through human-made technology, part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: However, presence means that our perception should be as good as perceiving reality. That means we should not be able to distinguish between our perception of stimuli generated by a computer vis-à-vis our perception of stimuli generated from the real world.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: So, in other words, we can say that the computer is generating stimuli which are stimulating our sensory organs, but we fail to acknowledge that that these are generated by a computer; instead, we perceive them to be coming from the real world.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: So with this knowledge, we can say that the overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, or in other words, to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world, but they are unable to distinguish between the real world and the virtual world.

questions.question: what is a matched zone
questions.reference_answer: The matched zone is the place where the real and the virtual world perfectly align: a region of the real world in which the user can physically move (the movement is confined to this safe region) and which is also a part of the virtual world, so physical motion there is matched by the same motion in the virtual world. Each user has their own matched zone; moving beyond it needs locomotion techniques.
must_have: a region where the real and the virtual world align
the user's physical movement is limited to it, and it is also part of the virtual world

sources.title: VR Software
sources.quote: So, there is something called a matched zone that is a place where real and virtual worlds perfectly align. So, this is a part of the, say, virtual world, but the user can move within this space in the real world and this movement is translated to the other parts of the virtual world. So, this region where the user's physical movement is restricted and which is also a part of the virtual world is called a matched zone.

sources.title: VR Software
sources.quote: In many VR experiences, users want to move well outside of the matched zone. Which motivates locomotion.

sources.title: VR Software
sources.quote: Each user has a distinct matched zone.

questions.question: What is the uncanny valley effect?
questions.reference_answer: The uncanny valley effect is the finding that digital representations of humans that look almost real evoke unease or eeriness instead of familiarity, because of subtle imperfections. As human likeness rises, familiarity rises, but at about 70 to 85 percent likeness it drops before rising again: that dip is the uncanny valley. The study was originally about robots. For VR it means that pushing for realism does not always give a better experience.
must_have: almost-real human representations cause unease / eeriness instead of familiarity
familiarity drops in a range of high human likeness (about 70-85%)

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

questions.question: What is usability?
questions.reference_answer: The course uses the ISO definition (ISO 9241-210): usability is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use. Effectiveness: can the users do what they want to do; efficiency: how fast; satisfaction: how satisfied they are while using it.

questions.question: What is a game engine?
questions.reference_answer: A game engine is a middleware on which the developer's application runs. It bundles several engines, typically a rendering engine, a physics engine, an audio engine and a user interface, with core functions such as rendering, physics, audio, scripting and networking support; an authoring tool gives access to them. Examples named: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, Amazon Sumerian. In the course a game engine serves as a ready-made virtual world generator for VR.

questions.question: what is contextual inquiry?
questions.reference_answer: Contextual inquiry is a method to gather end-user (usability) requirements. It is a semi-structured interview process made of observation and interviews: the designers watch users perform their tasks in their natural work setting and ask questions to clarify what they see. The observer acts as an apprentice and treats the user as the master (master-apprentice model).

questions.question: How does tracking work? What are the steps?
questions.reference_answer: Tracking works in four broad steps. Calibration: the sensor output is transformed to be as close to the real value as possible, since no sensor is perfect. Registration: the initial position and orientation of the sensor are determined. Integration: the sensor measurements, taken at discrete points of time and possibly from several sensors, are combined to follow what is tracked. Drift correction: the difference between the estimated and the actual position and orientation is compensated.
must_have: the four steps: calibration, registration, integration, drift correction

sources.quote: First is calibration, then registration, integration, and drift correction.

sources.title: Understanding Tracking I
sources.quote: In this step, what we do is estimate or determine the initial sensor position and orientation.

sources.title: Understanding Tracking I

sources.title: Understanding Tracking I

questions.question: How is drift corrected when tracking with an IMU?
questions.reference_answer: Drift correction compensates the error between the estimated and the actual orientation, and it needs at least one extra sensor besides the gyroscope: in an IMU the accelerometer and the magnetometer, or a separate camera. A classic approach blends the two separately computed orientations at the same instant with a gain parameter alpha between 0 and 1: corrected orientation = alpha x (orientation from integrating the gyroscope) + (1 - alpha) x (orientation from the other sensor).

questions.question: How can I tell whether some system is a VR system or not?
questions.reference_answer: Check it against the three defining characteristics of VR: (1) an artificial, computer-generated environment, (2) an immersive experience through computer-generated stimuli to the sense organs, (3) interactivity: the environment changes with the user's actions. A system is VR only if it has all three. Examples in the lecture: a CAD system (virtual and interactive but not immersive), a video conference (interactive only) and a 3D movie (virtual, partly immersive, not interactive) are not VR.

questions.question: how does marker based AR work
questions.reference_answer: A marker-based AR application uses markers placed in the environment to trigger the augmentation. When the device is pointed at a marker and detects it, the digital content is placed at the marker on the screen view of the real world. Markers can be QR codes, colour codes or bars, or fiducial markers. Such applications are easy to build but hard to maintain, because markers are prone to damage.

questions.question: How does the virtual world generator work?
questions.reference_answer: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the VR software, treated as a black box. It receives input events from low-level systems (head tracker, keyboard, mouse, game controller), which arrive in a queue. Its key role is to maintain enough of an internal reality: it keeps the virtual world in step with the input so that the renderers (visual, aural, haptic) can compute matching output for the displays. Its basic operation is to keep the user's motions in the real and the virtual world in correspondence. For this it must support the virtual world (graphics, or a captured world), matched motion, locomotion, physics and networked experiences.

takes input events from trackers / input devices

questions.question: How does the Wizard of Oz method work?
questions.reference_answer: In a Wizard of Oz experiment the user believes they are using a working system, while a hidden human (the wizard) produces the system's responses. In the lecture's example the subject speaks into a microphone and thinks the computer converts speech to text; in fact the wizard, hidden behind a wall, hears the speech, types it, and the text appears on the subject's screen. So an idea can be tested with users before the technology exists.

questions.question: How is a heuristic evaluation carried out?
questions.reference_answer: Heuristic evaluation is an expert (quick) evaluation technique: a prototype is evaluated against a checklist whose items are called heuristics. No scenario or task description is needed; the system is judged as a whole. A team of three to five evaluators, usually design team members or people familiar with the problem, each evaluate independently and report a list of usability issues. A general checklist is Nielsen's 10 heuristics.

questions.question: How do you find the best tour path when the user should not stay in VR longer than a time limit?
questions.reference_answer: The virtual world is modelled as a weighted graph whose nodes are the points of interest. A time threshold is set (above it cybersickness may occur). As not every node can then be visited, each node gets an importance (a positive number) and a waiting time. The task is to find a path that maximises the total importance while travel time plus waiting time stays within the threshold. This is a vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP): the graph is made complete with hypothetical edges, edge weights are set to travel times from the natural walking model, an existing VRPP solver is run, and hypothetical edges in the result are replaced by shortest paths.
must_have: a time threshold on the tour (to limit cybersickness)
nodes (points of interest) have an importance; maximise total importance within the time limit
solved as a vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) with an existing solver

sources.title: VR experience optimisation

In other words, we want to basically identify a path which takes time less than or equal to the threshold time, but in which we are maximizing the total importance.

sources.quote: So, essentially what we want to state is TP plus WP must be less than or equal to T threshold, where we are also maximizing FP.

questions.question: What is the difference between AR and VR?
questions.reference_answer: VR completely replaces the user's perception of the real world with a virtual environment; AR alters (augments, enhances) the ongoing perception of the real world with digital content. So VR needs nothing real to exist, while AR needs the real scene: in the lecture's example, a building that is not yet built can be walked through in VR, but for AR the building must exist, and virtual furniture can then be shown in its rooms.

questions.question: How are immersion and presence related?
questions.reference_answer: Immersion is objective and quantifiable: what the system provides (the technological side). Presence is a state of consciousness, the psychological sense of being in the virtual environment; it is inside the user's mind and hard to measure objectively. Immersion aids presence and limits it (more immersion, more potential presence), but does not guarantee it: a user who shuts their eyes has immersion without presence. Presence is a function of both the user and the immersion.
must_have: immersion: objective, what the technology provides
presence: subjective, psychological sense of being there

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: Immersion can be an objective and quantifiable description of what any particular system can provide or does provide, whereas presence is a state of consciousness or the psychological sense of being in the virtual environment.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: It is difficult to objectively measure. So, subjective experience has to be taken into account.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: Now, as is probably obvious by now, presence can be a function of both the user, that is the subjective experience, as well as immersion, that is the objective or technological experience.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: So, immersion aids presence, but it does not mean that if we provide immersive technology, then presence will automatically happen. Immersion is capable of producing presence, but not necessarily always.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: The greater immersion a system or application provides, the greater potential for a user to feel present in that virtual world.

questions.question: inside-out vs outside-in tracking: what's the difference?
questions.reference_answer: The difference is where the sensors are. In outside-in tracking the sensors (or markers) are external to the device, placed in the environment; tracking only works inside the area covered by them. In inside-out tracking the cameras or other sensors are in the device itself (for VR, the HMD), no external device is needed, and the user can go anywhere. Examples of inside-out: Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, Qualcomm VR820.
must_have: outside-in: sensors in the environment, external to the device
inside-out: sensors on the device the user wears

questions.question: Is mixed reality the same thing as augmented reality?
questions.reference_answer: In this course, yes: MR is treated as another term for AR. The lecture notes that practitioners do not agree on a definition of MR and lists several: everything between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum (so AR is part of MR); a combination of AR and VR in one app or device; a 'strong', more capable AR with an advanced understanding of the physical environment; or simply a synonym of AR. The course takes the last one for simplicity.

the course uses MR and AR interchangeably (same technology)
at least one other definition, e.g. everything between real and virtual on the continuum

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: I repeat, there is no agreement among practitioners on what exactly MR is. So, there is no agreement on the precise definition of the term MR.

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: MR is everything in between. the two extremes in the reality-virtuality continuum.

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: Sometimes mixed reality is also defined as a combination of AR and VR. In this case, MR denotes the capability to combine both technologies, AR and VR, in the same app or on the same device.

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: Yet another definition is MR is nothing but a strong AR. Now, as per this definition, MR is a more capable version of AR where an advanced understanding of the physical environment is present, which might be bound to specific hardware.

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: Finally, many people have also used these two terms interchangeably. That means, MR is nothing but a synonym for AR.

sources.title: Definitions
sources.quote: In subsequent lectures, we shall use the terms interchangeably. We will assume that MR is nothing but another term for AR. So AR and MR represent the same technology.

questions.question: What's the difference between augmented reality and augmented virtuality?
questions.reference_answer: They are opposites on the reality-virtuality continuum. In augmented reality the real world is augmented with virtual (digital) content; in augmented virtuality the virtual world is augmented with real-world content, for example a real human figure shown inside a virtual environment. The whole space between the fully real and the fully virtual environment is broadly called mixed reality.
must_have: AR: real world + virtual content
augmented virtuality: virtual world + real-world content

sources.title: General Intro to XR
sources.quote: In between, there is an interval where at one end we have augmented reality, that means we are augmenting the real world with some digital content, virtual content and at the other end there is augmented virtuality. This is just the opposite of augmented reality where we are augmenting the virtual world with real world content.

sources.title: General Intro to XR

sources.title: General Intro to XR

sources.title: General Intro to XR

questions.question: horizontal prototype vs vertical prototype?
questions.reference_answer: A horizontal prototype shows the whole interface at the surface level without functionality: only the look and feel is prototyped, not the interaction, so no real work can be done with it. A vertical prototype represents the interactions or functionalities, and suits the analysis of interactions and features. A single sketch is a horizontal prototype; a series of sketches (a storyboard) can act as a vertical one.

questions.question: What is the difference between a within-subject and a between-subject design?
questions.reference_answer: In a within-subject (repeated measures) design every participant performs the tasks for all test conditions. In a between-subjects design the tasks for the test conditions are divided among the participants, so not everyone does everything. Within-subject designs are easier to manage but can suffer from the practice effect, which adds noise to the data.

between-subjects: conditions are split among participants

sources.title: System Implementation

So, in a within-subject design, experimental design, or a repeated measures experimental design, all the participants are given all the tasks.

sources.title: System Implementation
sources.quote: So, when we distribute the tasks to participants, we call the study between-subjects. So, in the case of a between-subjects experimental design, not all participants get to perform all the tasks corresponding to all the test conditions.

sources.title: System Implementation

questions.question: How do rods and cones differ?
questions.reference_answer: Both are photoreceptors in the retina. Rods are more numerous in the peripheral region; cones are mainly in the small central region, the fovea. Several rods can share one optic nerve, while each cone can have its own, which aids acuity. Vision with cones only is photopic vision, which gives colour perception; vision with rods only is scotopic vision.
must_have: both are photoreceptors of the retina
cones: concentrated in the fovea, colour (photopic) vision
rods: periphery, scotopic vision

sources.title: Visual Perception & Displays I
sources.quote: Rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina, and cones are mainly in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.

sources.title: Visual Perception & Displays I
sources.quote: So, there can be multiple rods sharing one optic nerve whereas there can be one optic nerve for each cone which aids in image resolution and or In other words, which aids in acuity, image acuity.

sources.title: Visual Perception & Displays I
sources.quote: So, when we perceive something only with cones, vision accomplished only with cones, that is photopic vision. And when we perceive something with rods only, that is scotopic.

sources.title: Visual Perception & Displays I
sources.quote: So, when we say that we are perceiving color, we have to keep in mind that that is due to the photopic vision accomplished with cones.

questions.question: Travel and wayfinding - are they the same?
questions.reference_answer: No, they are the two components of navigation. Travel (locomotion) is the motor component: the actual movement from one location to another. Wayfinding is about knowing where one is and working out a path to the destination: building a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings. Without wayfinding support, travel techniques cannot be used efficiently in a complex environment.
must_have: both are components of navigation
travel / locomotion: the motor part, the movement itself
wayfinding: location awareness and finding the path (cognitive map)

sources.title: System Design

Now, travel is the motor component of navigation.

sources.title: System Design
sources.quote: So, there are two components of navigation: one is locomotion or travel, that is the motor component and The second component is wayfinding.

sources.title: System Design
sources.quote: Now, wayfinding refers to many things such as location awareness where one is located, and ascertaining a path through the environment to the desired destination. transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

sources.title: System Design
sources.quote: So, the goal of wayfinding is basically to build a mental model or a cognitive map of the surroundings as well as the overall environment so that it is easier for us to locate ourselves in the environment as well as to identify a suitable path to take us to the destination.

sources.title: System Design
sources.quote: So without suitable wayfinding support in a complex environment, irrespective of how many different types of traveling techniques are implemented, the user will not be able to perform efficient movement.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of an AR system?

The lecture then summarises four: the real world is enhanced with computer-generated content; the enhancement is registered in 3D (it appears at its appropriate place); the enhancement is experienced through the sense organs; and it supports interaction. A system is AR only if all are satisfied.

sources.title: Definitions

questions.question: List the types of AR applications.
questions.reference_answer: By technology there are two broad categories: marker-based and markerless AR applications. Markerless ones have four subcategories: location-based (a sensor such as GPS gives the user's location), superimposition-based (objects are recognised and content is superimposed), projection-based (light projectors put content on objects or surfaces) and outlining-based (object recognition is used to outline the surroundings, e.g. cars in low light).

the markerless subcategories: location-based, superimposition, projection-based, outlining

sources.title: Application Domains and System Categories

questions.question: what are the six qualities of immersion?
questions.reference_answer: Extensive (the range of sensory modalities presented), matching (congruence between modalities, e.g. the view follows head motion), surrounding (how panoramic the cues are, e.g. a wide field of view), vivid (the quality of energy within a modality: resolution, lighting, frame rate, audio bitrate), interactive (the user can change the world and influence future events) and plot informing (the user can follow the story of the experience).

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: The quality of energy stimulated within a particular modality.

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

sources.title: Issues & Challenges

sources.title: Issues & Challenges
sources.quote: The plot informing quality refers to our ability to understand the overall story, not only the current instance of what is happening, but the overall story, the overall script.

questions.question: What are the phases in the history of VR?
questions.reference_answer: Four phases: the early era, before digital computers (e.g. Wheatstone's stereoscope of 1838); the formative years, roughly 1950 to 1990 (Sensorama, Sutherland's Sword of Damocles, the term 'virtual reality'); the modern phase, 1991 to 2015 (CAVE, VRML, Oculus Rift); and the growth phase from 2016 onwards, which is the current one.
must_have: early era (before computers)
formative years (about 1950-1990)
modern phase (about 1991-2015)
growth phase (2016 onwards)

sources.title: Historical Evolution

So, we can call it the early era, then we have the formative years. which roughly we can associate with the years between 1950 and 1990. Then we have the modern phase between 1991 to 2015 and the growth phase, which is the current phase where we are all in, which roughly we can say started from 2016 onwards.

sources.title: Historical Evolution
sources.quote: Then there are the other three phases. formative years, modern phase, and growth phase.

sources.title: Historical Evolution
sources.quote: The first of those was developed in 1838 by Sir Charles Wheatstone, who demonstrated a stereoscopic device and established for the first time in recorded history that our brain can process 2D images as 3D objects.

The life cycle is highly iterative: there are loops between the stages to take in user feedback.

questions.question: What are the stages of the 3D graphics pipeline?
questions.reference_answer: Five stages: (1) object representation, (2) modeling transformation (local to world coordinates), (3) lighting, (4) the viewing pipeline, with the sub-stages viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation and window-to-viewport transformation, and (5) scan conversion (rendering, rasterization). An implementation need not follow exactly this order.

questions.question: HRTF?
questions.reference_answer: HRTF stands for head-related transfer function. It models how we receive sound from a location in space; a pair of HRTFs, one per ear, can be used to synthesize binaural sound, so that sound sources can be localised in an XR system. It depends on the size and shape of the head, ears and ear canal, so every person has a unique HRTF; in practice one for an average listener is used.

questions.question: what is an imu sensor
questions.reference_answer: IMU stands for inertial measurement unit: a composite piece of hardware with three types of sensors, found in many HMDs and mobile phones. The gyroscope captures angular velocity, the accelerometer linear acceleration along the three axes, and the magnetometer the magnetic field strength along the three axes. Tracking with an IMU relies mainly on the gyroscope; the other two help detect and correct drift.

questions.question: what is the go go techneque?
